narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 64% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. While the average student who is accepted ranks around the middle of their class, you placed in the bottom decile. This was the most important reason the model saw a high risk of not passing the bar.

Your LSAT score was the second most important factor and also increased the likelihood of failure. At 20, it sits well below the average of 37 among accepted students, signaling weaker preparation for the exam.

Your undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction. At 2.70 it is below the accepted average of 3.23, yet the model still treated this value as a modest positive signal that slightly reduced the predicted chance of failure. However, this encouraging element was not nearly enough to offset the two stronger negative signals.

Your family income, gender, race, and plans to attend full-time were not used by the model.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. These steps would directly address the factors that most hurt your current prediction. (218 words)
